questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: First of all I wanted to go somewhere where I spoke the language. Therefore, I considered English and German speaking countries. I also wanted to go to a country that is safe and not too unfamiliar - so I applied to universities in Canada, Switzerland, Germany, and Scotland. The University of British Columbia seemed like the best option in Canada for me. UBC is a great academic institution with massive facilities, it has a beautiful modern campus right next to the Sea, it is in the big city of Vancouver - but by itself, which makes it even safer than the city. The campus life here is completely different to University of Copenhagen, since everything at UBC is in one place. You naturally to meet students that study completely different things to yourself, which is so fun. At UCPH I mostly spend time with students that study the same thing as me, and I'm very happy to have close friends that I spend a lot of time with there, but it is different at UBC. Since the students at UBC are always mixed up they have a lot of friends, however they don't have that many close friends, this makes it a good place to study abroad since people are very open and used to making new friends, so if you're open yourself it is super easy to make friends here. UBC also has a lot of clubs and campus activities. I myself became a member of the Varsity Outdoor Club, which was great fun. I went on a lot of trips in the weekends with other students who enjoy getting out and exploring nature. The club has some super advanced trips, but I mostly did beginner friendly ones. Becoming a member also means that you can rent gear for free. If you're not a hiker, skier, or snowshoer there are also 300+ other clubs you could join, and I'd highly recommend taking a look at the ones you find interesting, since the people running the clubs are always very passionate and love when potential new members show interest - so don't be shy! As I mentioned they also have a lot of campus activities, the UBC Thunderbirds have sports teams in Hockey, American Football, Basketball, and much more. As a student it's free to go to these games and if you bring along some friends it can definitely be a fun experience. The only thing I was worried about when coming here was the long distance away from home, but I honestly haven't felt it at all.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy. I was just sent emails with what I had to do.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I recieved help finding my room once I arrived in residence, and the first few days there was a big introduction to studying at UBC, where all exchange students were also shown around campus to get familiar with it, which also meant we met many other exchangers so to make new friends. We were also introduced to all the clubs and so on, so I felt very welcomed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I applied for housing, where I had to set my priority list of the different options. I generally chose options to live alone over options to live with others. They say that there is around a 50 % chance that you get a spot in residence, and I was one of the lucky ones that did. It saves sooo much time and also money, since living in Vancouver is further away and often more expensive, as well as being super difficult to actually find a place. I ended up living at Walter Gage in a 6 bedroom apartment, and I'm honestly happy that I got to stay in a place with roomates. I became great friends with the other exchange students in my apartment and even though sharing a kitchen can be a bit tough it didn't matter too much, since most of my time was spent outside the dorm. Also they give most exchange students the apartments at the top of Walter Gage, which meant I had a view over the Burrard Inlet, Bowen Island as well as the Mountains north of Vancouver, something most five star hotels can't even dream of.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You can get a meal plan but it is made for first year students who live in residence where they don't have have kitchen. Most options for residence have a kitchen so that you can cook yourself, there are also many resturaunts around campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I did usually cook meals myself. However they were simple and easy meals so it didn't take a lot of time to make them. Most of my roomates did the same as me, however one of my canadian roomates had these meal boxes come each week where he had to cook the food that they planned for him (not from UBC it was a private company), and he spent sooo much time in the kitchen, which was a bit annoying for both him and us. I also often ate out with friends, which I would recommend since it is a bit cheaper here compared to Denmark, though when you see the prices tax isn't included, and they expect a 15 % tip aswell.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: For me personally it was a 5, however since only around 50 % of exchangers get housing from UBC it can really be a pain if you don't get it - from what I've heard. That's why I'm giving it a 4 instead.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to tell Go Global what you wanted to be registered for and then they would do it for you. It could be a pain if you wanted to take very popular courses since they were not that fast. Also if you wanted a graduate course the process was a bit more complicated where you might even have to write the professor an email yourself. So the process wasn't ideal, however they explained everything very well in great detail, so you just had to follow their instructions, and they were also good at answering any questions.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Go Global helps all the exchangers get their desired courses. However they can't guarentee anything, so you have to find backup courses, if you didn't get the ones that you wanted the most.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had some that I initially wanted, that were only offered in the second term so I couldn't get those, but of the ones that actually got offered in the first term, I got the 5 I wanted the most, and then dropped one so that I only had 4 courses, which is what I needed to get 30 ECTS.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just keep up to date on the courses they are offering, check what they offered last year, and follow the instructions of Go Global. You might have to submit your pre-approval to UCPH before you're actually registered for courses, so just add as many courses as you can. I even registered twice, just for extra security.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I'm a in my third and final year of my BA at UCPH. At UBC it is common to go work right after your Undergrad and not do a Masters. It is also a 4 year Undergrad, since they start 1 year earlier at uni than we do in Denmark. At UBC I took 300 and 400 level courses, which are made for 3rd and 4th year students. This made a lot of sense. The level of 4th year courses at UBC was similar to 3rd year courses at UCPH and the 3rd year courses at UBC was about the same as 2nd year courses at UCPH, so it matched quite well. And taking some courses that were a bit easier was nice, since I had more time to explore British Columbia.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I study physics at home and took physics courses at UBC. Usually we have a lot of tutorials at home here we didn't have any tutorials, we still had problems to do, but you had to do them more on your own, which was nice for me since it made my schedule more flexible.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: PHYS 407 Introduction to General Relativity, PHYS 400 Introduction to Elementary Particles, PHYS 315 Quantum Physics of Materials, and PHYS 312 Introduction to Mathematical Physics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: PHYS 315 was very nice as an exchange student, since the course was very easy to get a good grade in, but I still felt like I learned alot. If you want a challenge then PHYS 400 is a good one, since it is an undergrad/grad course, so the class is small, the level is high, and there is sooo much material.

questions.answer: Most items are less expensive some are the same price, however tax is not included in the price you see when buying.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Over 300+ clubs + loads of on campus activities aranged by the university, the housing, or one of the clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: VOC - Go on hikes. You can plan your own trips, but going with the VOC is so nice, since someone will have planned the trip for you, and they are often experienced, so it's almost guarenteed that it will be a success.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If the weather isn't great you can go to a Whitecaps game, it isn't as expensive as you'd expect. You can also watch the Canucks, but that is more expensive. There are loads of fun museums around campus that are free as a UBC student. And then go on trips, Vancouver Island is very nice. Banff and Jasper isn't very far either. There are also loads of beautiful hikes near Vancouver.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is very international, so not difficult at all.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to all the activities and clubs that you find somewhat interesting.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really any.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How open a lot of people are when you first meet them.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Apply for housing and have backup plans. Look at what you want to do before you get there - find a few objectives you wanna conquer. Be open and talk to people about their passions.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nah, you're good.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I met and the experiences I had - especially in nature.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Overcoming the barrier of asking people to do stuff, but also doing stuff by yourself.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
